proofs.proof_tex:
Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  Because a triangular matrix and each of its powers have diagonal entries equal to the corresponding powers of the original diagonal entries,
\[
 B_{ii}=(A^m)_{ii}=A_{ii}^m.
\]
The map \(x\mapsto x^m\) is one-to-one on \(\mathbb R\) for odd \(m\), so necessarily
\[
 A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m}
\]
for every \(i\).  Thus every compatible pair has the same diagonal transition coefficients.

Proceed by induction on the endpoint gap \(g=i-j\ge1\).  All entries of gap zero have just been determined.  Suppose all allowed entries of gap less than \(g\) have been determined.  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) gives, for an allowed edge \(j\to i\) of gap \(g\),
\[
 B_{ij}=A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})+R_{ij,m}(A).
\]
Every off-diagonal factor in \(R_{ij,m}(A)\) has gap less than \(g\), so the induction hypothesis determines the remainder.  By the hypothesis on allowed edges and Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}divided\mbox{-}difference\mbox{-}zero\mbox{-}set}\),
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})>0.
\]
Division is therefore valid and forces
\[
 A_{ij}=\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})}.
\]
For a forbidden pair, graph support forces \(A_{ij}=0\), and the same path expansion turns the equality \(A^m=B\) at that coordinate into the check \(B_{ij}=R_{ij,m}(A)\).  Induction over \(g=1,\ldots,d-1\) proves that there is at most one graph-compatible \(A\) and gives the asserted recursion.

Fix this \(A\).  Since \(D\) is diagonal, the \((i,i)\) entry of the coarse covariance equation is
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{d}D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
Lower triangularity gives \((A^r)_{ij}=0\) for \(j>i\), while \((A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r\).  Hence
\[
 Q_{ii}
 =D_{ii}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
  +\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^{2}.
\]
The coefficient of \(D_{ii}\) is at least its \(r=0\) term, namely one.  Starting at \(i=1\) and increasing \(i\), division therefore uniquely yields exactly the displayed innovation recursion.  Thus there is at most one diagonal \(D\).

For sufficiency, construct \(A\) and \(D\) by these recursions.  The diagonal and allowed-coordinate equations for \(A^m=B\) hold by construction; imposing the forbidden-coordinate checks gives the full equation \(A^m=B\).  The diagonal covariance equations hold by construction; imposing the remaining entries gives the full equation \(Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top\).  The graph zeros are built into \(A\).  The explicit stability and positivity checks give \(\max_i|A_{ii}|<1\) and diagonal \(D\succ0\), respectively.  These are precisely all conditions in \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), proving sufficiency.  Necessity of each check follows immediately from the definition of that fiber.  It follows that every nonempty fiber is a singleton.

Finally, \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is the image of the compatible fiber under
\[
 (A,D)\longmapsto \left[z\longmapsto\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}\right].
\]
Stability gives \(|A_{vv}z|<1\) for \(|z|=1\), so the denominator never vanishes.  The singleton parameter fiber therefore maps to the singleton containing the causal transfer \(h_{uv}\), rather than defining that causal transfer from the observed law.

For an exact two-node stress test satisfying the regularity condition, take \(m=3\),
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\1/4&1/3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad D=I_2.
\]
Then \(B_{11}=1/8\), \(B_{22}=1/27\), and, since there is no indirect path,
\[
 B_{21}=\frac14 C_3(1/3,1/2)
 =\frac14\left(\frac19+\frac16+\frac14\right)=\frac{19}{144}.
\]
The formula recovers \(A_{21}=(19/144)/(19/36)=1/4\), and the covariance recursion recovers both entries of \(D=I_2\), so the recovered transfer is \(z/[4(1-z/3)]\).  The excluded condition is load-bearing: with
\[
 A(a)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\a&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1),
\]
where \(q_1,q_2>0\) and \(|a|<\sqrt{q_2/q_1}\), one has \(A(a)^3=0\) and
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A(a)^rD(a)(A(a)^r)^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2).
\]
Thus the same coarse law admits an open interval of transfers \(az\) when both endpoint persistences vanish.

Write
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}
 (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)
\]
and let \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) denote the target-corridor class in \(\mathrm{def{:}corridor\mbox{-}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class}\) with the same arguments.  By \(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}class}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}class}\), every \(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) belongs to the compact class, has odd \(m\), and satisfies
\[
 m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa\quad(i\in V),
 \qquad
 |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa\quad(j\to i\in E).
\]
Since \(V_{uv}^{G}\subseteq V\) and \(E_{uv}^{G}\subseteq E\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}target\mbox{-}corridor}\), restriction of these inequalities gives
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}\subseteq\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}.             \tag{1}
\]
The displayed feasibility condition in the theorem and \(\mathrm{lem{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}nonempty}\) give \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\ne\varnothing\), so the global uniform assertion is nonvacuous.

It remains only to compare the two estimators.  On any neighborhood where the global recursion is defined, \(\mathrm{lem{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion\mbox{-}closure}\) shows inductively that the global and corridor recursions produce identical values for every corridor diagonal and corridor edge: each such update has the same numerator, denominator, and previously recovered inputs.  In particular,
\[
 \widehat A_{vu}^{\mathrm{global}}=\widehat A_{vu}^{\mathrm{cor}},
 \qquad
 \widehat A_{vv}^{\mathrm{global}}=\widehat A_{vv}^{\mathrm{cor}},
 \qquad
 \widehat h_{uv}=\widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}.                       \tag{2}
\]
On \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\), all population diagonal-root derivatives and all global divided differences are at least \(\kappa\) in absolute value.  Consistency of \(\widehat B\), supplied by \(\mathrm{thm{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}wald\mbox{-}band}\), therefore makes the event on which both recursions are defined in a common \(\kappa/2\)-neighborhood have probability tending to one uniformly.  Their arbitrary definitions off this event do not change any limit.

Differentiating the identical target formulas in \((2)\) shows that the target rows of the global and corridor Jacobians coincide; the closure lemma also shows that these rows have zero derivative with respect to every off-corridor input.  Hence the positive-semidefinite plug-in covariance and the Gaussian maximum-modulus critical value in the present statement agree with their corridor counterparts with probability tending to one uniformly.  Applying \(\mathrm{thm{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}wald\mbox{-}band}\) and then restricting its supremum using \((1)\) proves the asserted Gaussian limit and simultaneous coverage formula.  Thus the global regular Wald theorem is a nonvacuous corollary of the target-corridor inference result.

added_lemmas.statement: If \(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}\), then every strict edge and every vertex occurring in a monomial of \(R_{ij,m}(A)\) lies in \(E_{uv}^{G}\) and \(V_{uv}^{G}\), respectively.  Every strict edge in such a monomial has endpoint gap strictly smaller than \(i-j\).  Consequently the recursion for a corridor edge uses only corridor diagonal entries and previously recovered corridor edges.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}target\mbox{-}corridor}\), there is a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\) that contains the edge \(j\to i\).  In particular there are directed paths \(u\leadsto j\) and \(i\leadsto v\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\), a monomial of \(R_{ij,m}(A)\) is indexed by a nondecreasing walk from \(j\) to \(i\) with at least two strict increases, and every strict increase follows an edge of \(G\).  Delete the repeated vertices caused by diagonal steps.  The remaining strict steps form a directed path
\[
 j=i_0\to i_1\to\cdots\to i_r=i,
 \qquad r\ge2.
\]
Concatenating \(u\leadsto j\), this path, and \(i\leadsto v\) gives a directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path.  Hence each \(i_\ell\) belongs to \(V_{uv}^{G}\), and every edge \(i_{\ell-1}\to i_\ell\) belongs to \(E_{uv}^{G}\), by the same definition.  Because \(r\ge2\) and the supplied labels increase strictly along every edge, for every \(\ell\)
\[
 0<i_\ell-i_{\ell-1}<i-j.
\]
Thus all off-diagonal factors of the monomial have smaller endpoint gap.  Diagonal factors use only the vertices \(i_\ell\) already shown to lie in the corridor.  This holds for every monomial, proving all three claims.

added_lemmas.statement:
Suppose \(m\) is odd, \(u\to v\in G\), and \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\ne\varnothing\).  If
\[
 C_m(B_{ii}^{1/m},B_{jj}^{1/m})\ne0
 \qquad\text{for every }j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G},
\]
then all compatible pairs \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) have the same diagonal coordinates \(A_{ii}\), \(i\in V_{uv}^{G}\), and the same edge coordinates \(A_{ij}\), \(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}\).  These common coordinates equal \(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)\), and
\[
 \mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)=\{\Phi_{uv,m,G}(B)\}.
\]
No uniqueness is asserted for transition coordinates or innovation variances outside the target corridor.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix two arbitrary compatible pairs \((A,D),(\widetilde A,\widetilde D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  The lower-triangular restrictions in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) imply that the diagonal of a power is the corresponding power of the diagonal.  Therefore, for every \(i\in V\),
\[
 B_{ii}=(A^m)_{ii}=A_{ii}^m,
 \qquad
 B_{ii}=(\widetilde A^m)_{ii}=\widetilde A_{ii}^m.
\]
Because \(m\) is odd, the real map \(x\mapsto x^m\) is injective and surjective.  Hence
\[
 A_{ii}=\widetilde A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m}.                 \tag{1}
\]
In particular, all corridor diagonal entries agree with the first step of \(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)\).

We induct over the positive endpoint gap \(g=i-j\).  Suppose that every corridor edge of gap less than \(g\) has the same coefficient under \(A\) and \(\widetilde A\), equal to the corridor recursion.  For a corridor edge \(j\to i\) with \(i-j=g\), \(\mathrm{lem{:}path\mbox{-}expansion}\) gives
\[
 B_{ij}
 =A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})+R_{ij,m}(A),                  \tag{2}
\]
and the same identity with \(\widetilde A\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion\mbox{-}closure}\), every entry in the two remainders is either a corridor diagonal or a corridor edge of smaller gap.  Equation \((1)\) and the induction hypothesis therefore imply
\[
 R_{ij,m}(A)=R_{ij,m}(\widetilde A).                       \tag{3}
\]
The denominator in \((2)\) equals
\[
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})
 =C_m(B_{ii}^{1/m},B_{jj}^{1/m})\ne0                       \tag{4}
\]
by the displayed hypothesis.  Subtracting the common remainder and dividing by \((4)\) is legitimate, and yields
\[
 A_{ij}=\widetilde A_{ij}
 =\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(B_{ii}^{1/m},B_{jj}^{1/m})}.
                                                                    \tag{5}
\]
This is exactly the next step in \(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)\).  Finite induction proves equality of all stated corridor coordinates.  Notice that neither \((2)\)--\((5)\) nor the closure lemma uses any off-corridor coefficient.

The assumption \(u\to v\in G\) implies \(u\to v\in E_{uv}^{G}\) and \(v\in V_{uv}^{G}\).  Thus \((5)\) identifies \(A_{vu}\), while \((1)\) identifies \(A_{vv}\).  Every compatible pair consequently has the same causal transfer
\[
 h_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}
 =\frac{\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{vu}z}
 {1-\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{vv}z}
 =\Phi_{uv,m,G}(B)(z).                                    \tag{6}
\]
Compatibility includes \(|A_{vv}|<1\), so for \(|z|=1\),
\[
 |1-A_{vv}z|\ge1-|A_{vv}|>0,                              \tag{7}
\]
and the transfer in \((6)\) is defined on all of \(\mathbb T\).  By \(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}fiber}\), equality \((6)\) for every member of the nonempty compatible fiber is precisely
\(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)=\{\Phi_{uv,m,G}(B)\}\).  The argument did not compare any off-corridor coordinate or any component of \(D\), so it makes no claim that the full compatible fiber is a singleton.

The localization is strict.  Take \(d=4\), \(m=3\), let \(G\) have only the edges \(1\to3\) and \(2\to4\), and query \(1\to3\).  With
\[
 A_{11}=\frac12,\quad A_{33}=\frac13,\quad A_{31}=\frac14,
 \qquad A_{22}=A_{44}=A_{42}=0,
\]
and any positive diagonal \(D\), the target corridor is \(\{1,3\}\) with its single edge.  Its divisor is
\[
 C_3(1/3,1/2)=\frac19+\frac16+\frac14=\frac{19}{36}>0,
\]
so the target is recovered as \(z/[4(1-z/3)]\).  The unrelated allowed edge \(2\to4\) has divisor \(C_3(0,0)=0\), so the global noncollision condition fails while the corridor conclusion remains valid.  Conversely, if the queried two-node block has
\[
 A(a)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\a&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1),
 \qquad |a|<\sqrt{q_2/q_1},
\]
then \(A(a)^3=0\), \(D(a)\succ0\), and
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A(a)^rD(a)(A(a)^r)^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2).
\]
The same coarse law therefore attains the open family of transfers \(az\).  This failure occurs exactly at the corridor divisor \(C_3(0,0)=0\), showing that the localized division premise is load-bearing.

added_lemmas.statement:
For fixed \(d,m,G,\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max}\), uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\),
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}_{s}
 \bigl(\widehat M_0-M_0,\widehat M_1-M_1\bigr)
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Omega(P)),
 \qquad
 \Omega(P)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}_P(g_0,g_k),
\]
where
\[
 g_s=\operatorname{vec}_{s}
 \bigl(Y_sY_s^\top-M_0,Y_sY_{s-1}^\top-M_1\bigr).
\]
The covariance series converges absolutely and uniformly.  On the event that \(\widehat B=\widehat M_1\widehat M_0^{-1}\) exists and is stable, substituting \((\widehat B,\widehat M_0)\) into the Gaussian Isserlis covariance series and projecting onto the positive-semidefinite cone gives a uniformly consistent estimator of \(\Omega(P)\); defining it arbitrarily off that event does not affect consistency.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(\rho=1-\gamma<1\) and let \(\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{cmp}}\) denote the class in the statement.  We first derive uniform covariance decay from the defining bounds of \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\).  A nonzero entry of \(A^r\) is a sum over nondecreasing labeled walks.  Such a walk has at most \(d-1\) strict increases; every strict-increase factor has modulus at most \(L\), every diagonal factor has modulus at most \(\rho\), and the positions of the strict increases can be chosen in at most a polynomial number of ways.  Since \(d\) is fixed, there is a finite \(C_A=C_A(d,L,\rho)\) such that, uniformly over the class,
\[
 \lVert A^r\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le C_A(r+1)^{d-1}\rho^{(r-d+1)_+},
 \qquad r\ge0.                                             \tag{1}
\]
The innovation bounds in \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\) and the stationary series representation give
\[
 M_0=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}A^rD(A^r)^\top,
 \qquad
 d_{\min}I_d\preceq M_0\preceq C_0I_d                    \tag{2}
\]
for a finite \(C_0=C_0(d,L,\gamma,d_{\max})\); the lower inequality uses the \(r=0\) summand \(D\succeq d_{\min}I_d\), and the upper inequality follows by squaring and summing \((1)\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}coarse\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}reduction}\), the sampled process is the stationary Gaussian recursion
\[
 Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s,
 \qquad B=A^m,
 \qquad \eta_s\mathrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim N(0,Q),           \tag{3}
\]
with each \(\eta_s\) independent of the preceding coarse history.  Hence, for \(k\ge0\),
\[
 \Gamma_Y(k):=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_k,Y_0)=B^kM_0=A^{mk}M_0. \tag{4}
\]
Equations \((1)\), \((2)\), and transposition for negative lags imply constants \(C<\infty\) and \(r_0\in(0,1)\), depending only on the displayed class constants, such that
\[
 \lVert\Gamma_Y(k)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le C(|k|+1)^{d-1}r_0^{|k|},
 \qquad k\in\mathbb Z.                                    \tag{5}
\]

Let \(W_s=(Y_s^\top,Y_{s-1}^\top)^\top\).  Every coordinate of \(g_s\) is a centered product of two coordinates of \(W_s\).  For centered jointly Gaussian variables, expanding the fourth moment into its three pairings and subtracting the product of the two within-time covariances gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(W_{0,a}W_{0,b},W_{k,c}W_{k,e})
 =\operatorname{Cov}(W_{0,a},W_{k,c})
  \operatorname{Cov}(W_{0,b},W_{k,e})
 +\operatorname{Cov}(W_{0,a},W_{k,e})
  \operatorname{Cov}(W_{0,b},W_{k,c}).                     \tag{6}
\]
Each cross-covariance on the right is an entry of \(\Gamma_Y(k+s)\) for \(s\in\{-1,0,1\}\).  Thus \((5)\)--\((6)\) give
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
 \lVert\operatorname{Cov}_P(g_0,g_k)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le C_g(|k|+2)^{2d-2}r_0^{2(|k|-1)_+}.                   \tag{7}
\]
The right-hand side is summable over \(k\in\mathbb Z\), proving absolute and uniform convergence of \(\Omega(P)\).

We next prove the central limit assertion without adding a mixing hypothesis.  Fix a real vector \(t\) of the dimension of \(g_s\), and put
\[
 S_n(t)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}t^\top g_s.
\]
With \({\bf Y}_n=(Y_0^\top,\ldots,Y_n^\top)^\top\), there is a real symmetric block-banded matrix \(H_n(t)\), of bandwidth one, such that
\[
 S_n(t)=n^{-1/2}
 \left\{{\bf Y}_n^\top H_n(t){\bf Y}_n
 -\operatorname{tr}\bigl(H_n(t)\Gamma_n\bigr)\right\},
 \qquad \Gamma_n=\operatorname{Cov}({\bf Y}_n).            \tag{8}
\]
The finitely many block values of \(H_n(t)\) depend only on \(t\), so \(\sup_n\lVert H_n(t)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty\).  The block Toeplitz form of \(\Gamma_n\) and the summability in \((5)\) give, by the maximum block-row-sum bound,
\[
 \sup_{n\ge1}\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
 \lVert\Gamma_n\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty.               \tag{9}
\]
Let \(K_n=\Gamma_n^{1/2}H_n(t)\Gamma_n^{1/2}\), and let \(\mu_{n,1},\ldots,\mu_{n,(n+1)d}\) be its real eigenvalues.  Equations \((8)\)--\((9)\) imply \(\max_j|\mu_{n,j}|\le C_t\) uniformly.

To calculate the characteristic function, write \({\bf Y}_n=\Gamma_n^{1/2}\xi\) with \(\xi\sim N(0,I)\), allowing zero eigenvalues of \(\Gamma_n\), and diagonalize \(K_n\).  Independence of the coordinates of the rotated \(\xi\) and the elementary Gaussian integral
\[
 \mathbb E\exp(i a\xi_1^2)=(1-2ia)^{-1/2}
\]
give, for fixed \(\lambda\),
\[
 \mathbb E e^{i\lambda S_n(t)}
 =\prod_j
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{i\lambda\mu_{n,j}}{\sqrt n}\right)
 \left(1-\frac{2i\lambda\mu_{n,j}}{\sqrt n}\right)^{-1/2}. \tag{10}
\]
For all sufficiently large \(n\), uniformly in the model and in \(j\), the arguments of the logarithms in \((10)\) lie in a fixed disk not containing zero.  Taylor expansion of \(-\frac12\log(1-x)\), with the linear term canceled by the exponential, yields
\[
 \log\mathbb E e^{i\lambda S_n(t)}
 =-\frac{\lambda^2}{n}\sum_j\mu_{n,j}^2+\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 |\mathcal R_n|
 \le \frac{C_\lambda}{n^{3/2}}\sum_j|\mu_{n,j}|^3
 \le\frac{C_{\lambda,t}}{\sqrt n}.                        \tag{11}
\]
The finite-sample variance identity following from stationarity is
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_P(S_n(t))
 =\sum_{|k|<n}\left(1-\frac{|k|}{n}\right)
 t^\top\operatorname{Cov}_P(g_0,g_k)t
 =\frac{2}{n}\sum_j\mu_{n,j}^2.                            \tag{12}
\]
By the uniform summability in \((7)\), the first expression in \((12)\) converges uniformly to \(t^\top\Omega(P)t\).  Substitution into \((11)\) proves, uniformly in \(P\),
\[
 \mathbb E e^{i\lambda S_n(t)}
 -\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}t^\top\Omega(P)t\right)
 \longrightarrow0.                                        \tag{13}
\]
This remains valid when the limiting variance is zero.  Since \((13)\) holds for every fixed \(t\), the Cram\'er--Wold argument proves the asserted vector Gaussian limit uniformly.

It remains to establish the plug-in assertion.  The just-proved limit implies
\[
 \widehat M_0-M_0=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}),
 \qquad
 \widehat M_1-M_1=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})                  \tag{14}
\]
uniformly.  By \((2)\), matrix inversion is uniformly continuous on a common neighborhood of all population \(M_0\)'s.  Therefore
\[
 \widehat B-B=o_{\mathbb P}(1)                             \tag{15}
\]
uniformly.  Every population \(B=A^m\) has spectral radius at most \(\rho^m<1\).  The population \(B\)'s form a compact set, and the stable matrices form an open set, so they possess a common stable neighborhood.  Consequently
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
 P(\widehat B\text{ is not stable})\longrightarrow0.       \tag{16}
\]
On the complementary event, all covariances used in \((6)\) are explicit continuous functions of \((\widehat B,\widehat M_0)\): for nonnegative lag \(k\), use \(\widehat B^k\widehat M_0\), and use its transpose for negative lag.  Finite truncations of the Isserlis series are therefore uniformly consistent by \((14)\)--\((15)\).  On a sufficiently small common stable neighborhood, the same walk or Jordan-block estimate as in \((5)\) supplies a summable envelope independent of the model and of the estimate.  The tails of both the population and plug-in series are consequently uniformly negligible.  The unprojected Isserlis estimator \(\widetilde\Omega\) thus satisfies
\[
 \widetilde\Omega-\Omega(P)=o_{\mathbb P}(1)              \tag{17}
\]
uniformly.  Let \(\widehat\Omega\) be a closest positive-semidefinite matrix to \(\widetilde\Omega\) in Frobenius norm.  Since \(\Omega(P)\succeq0\), the minimizing property and the triangle inequality give
\[
 \lVert\widehat\Omega-\Omega(P)\rVert_F
 \le2\lVert\widetilde\Omega-\Omega(P)\rVert_F.           \tag{18}
\]
Equations \((16)\)--\((18)\) prove the stated uniform consistency, including the permitted arbitrary definition off the stable event.

added_lemmas.statement:
Suppose \(\mathcal Z\ne\varnothing\), \(m\) is odd, every arrow \(j\to i\) in \(G\) satisfies \(j<i\), \(u\to v\in G\), and
\[
 \kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal M_{uv,\mathrm{cor}}^{\partial}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)\) is nonempty.  Uniformly over this class, as \(n\to\infty\), the real vector stacking the real and imaginary parts of
\[
 \sqrt n\bigl(\widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}(z)-h_{uv}(z)\bigr),
 \qquad z\in\mathcal Z,
\]
converges to the centered Gaussian law obtained by applying the Jacobian of the moment-to-\(B\) map, the target-corridor recursion, and
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z\,\mathrm dA_{vu}}{1-A_{vv}z}
  +\frac{A_{vu}z^2\,\mathrm dA_{vv}}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}
\]
to the long-run Gaussian lag-moment covariance.  Let \(\widehat\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}\) be the positive-semidefinite plug-in estimate obtained from the Gaussian Isserlis covariance series and this localized Jacobian, and let \(\widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}\) be the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the maximum complex modulus of the corresponding centered Gaussian vector.  Then
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{uv,\mathrm{cor}}^{\partial}}
 \left|
 P\!\left\{
 h_{uv}(z)\in
 \left\{w\in\mathbb C:
 |w-\widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}(z)|
 \le\frac{\widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}}{\sqrt n}
 \right\}
 \text{ for every }z\in\mathcal Z
 \right\}-(1-\alpha)
 \right|\longrightarrow0,
\]
where the class in the supremum has the full argument list displayed above.  This result imposes no root-derivative or divided-difference separation outside \(V_{uv}^{G}\) and \(E_{uv}^{G}\), and does not assert full-\(A\) uniqueness.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Let
\[
 \mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{uv,\mathrm{cor}}^{\partial}
 (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa).
\]
We first verify nonemptiness and then prove the uniform limit.  Since \(m\ge2\) is odd, \(m\ge3\).  Put
\[
 a=\left(\frac{\kappa}{m}\right)^{1/(m-1)}.
\]
The displayed feasibility condition gives \(0<a\le1-\gamma\).  Let \(A=aI_d\) and \(D=d_{\min}I_d\), set every allowed off-diagonal coefficient to zero, and let \(X\) and \(Y\) be the stationary Gaussian processes generated by these parameters.  This choice obeys all graph zeros, \(|A_{ij}|\le L\) because \(a<1\le L\), and
\[
 d_{\min}I_d\preceq D=d_{\min}I_d\preceq d_{\max}I_d.
\]
It is stable because \(\rho(A)=a\le1-\gamma<1\).  For every vertex and every allowed edge,
\[
 m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}=ma^{m-1}=\kappa,
 \qquad
 C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})=C_m(a,a)=ma^{m-1}=\kappa.              \tag{1}
\]
In particular the localized inequalities hold, so \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\ne\varnothing\).  Conversely, because \(u\to v\in G\) implies \(u\in V_{uv}^{G}\), membership of any model in this class would give
\[
 \kappa\le m|A_{uu}|^{m-1}\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}.           \tag{2}
\]
Thus the displayed feasibility range is also necessary, although only sufficiency is needed below.

The parameter set underlying \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) is a closed subset of the compact coefficient set in \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\): graph zeros are closed, the entry and eigenvalue inequalities are closed and bounded, and the two localized inequalities are continuous polynomial inequalities over fixed finite sets.  Hence it is compact.  Each member determines a unique stationary Gaussian law because its triangular eigenvalues obey \(|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma<1\) and its innovations are Gaussian with \(D\succ0\).

Put
\[
 \vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(M_0,M_1),
 \qquad
 \widehat\vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(\widehat M_0,\widehat M_1).
\]
As in equations \((1)\)--\((2)\) of \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}compact\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\), there is a finite constant \(C_0=C_0(d,L,\gamma,d_{\max})\) such that, uniformly over the compact class,
\[
 d_{\min}I_d\preceq M_0\preceq C_0I_d.                    \tag{3}
\]
The moment-to-coarse-transition map is therefore twice continuously differentiable with uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on a common neighborhood:
\[
 (M_0,M_1)\longmapsto B=M_1M_0^{-1}.                       \tag{4}
\]

We next analyze the localized inverse.  For \(i\in V_{uv}^{G}\),
\[
 B_{ii}=A_{ii}^m,
 \qquad
 \left|\frac{\partial B_{ii}}{\partial A_{ii}}\right|
 =m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa.                               \tag{5}
\]
Oddness makes the real root unique.  Its first and second derivatives away from zero are
\[
 \frac{\partial A_{ii}}{\partial B_{ii}}
 =\frac{1}{mA_{ii}^{m-1}},
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial^2 A_{ii}}{\partial B_{ii}^2}
 =-\frac{m-1}{m^2A_{ii}^{2m-1}}.                           \tag{6}
\]
The first inequality in the definition of \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) gives \(|A_{ii}|\ge(\kappa/m)^{1/(m-1)}>0\), so both quantities in \((6)\) are uniformly bounded on the class.

For a corridor edge \(j\to i\), \(\mathrm{thm{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}identification}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion}\) give
\[
 A_{ij}
 =\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})},
 \qquad
 |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa.                            \tag{7}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion\mbox{-}closure}\), the polynomial remainder in \((7)\) uses only corridor diagonals and corridor edges of smaller endpoint gap.  Starting from \((6)\) and inducting over the finitely many gaps, every recovered corridor coordinate is therefore a twice continuously differentiable function of \(B\).  Compactness and continuity provide a common open neighborhood of the population \(B\)'s on which every divisor in \((5)\)--\((7)\) has absolute value at least \(\kappa/2\), and all first and second derivatives of the corridor recursion are uniformly bounded there.  This conclusion uses no off-corridor divisor.

For every \(z\in\mathcal Z\subset\mathbb T\), the stability margin supplies
\[
 |1-A_{vv}z|\ge1-|A_{vv}|\ge\gamma.                        \tag{8}
\]
Thus the transfer map is twice continuously differentiable on the same common neighborhood.  Direct differentiation gives
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z\,\mathrm dA_{vu}}{1-A_{vv}z}
  +\frac{A_{vu}z^2\,\mathrm dA_{vv}}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}.       \tag{9}
\]
Let \(F(\vartheta)\) stack the real and imaginary parts of \((h_{uv}(z))_{z\in\mathcal Z}\), and let \(J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(\vartheta)\) be the Jacobian of the composite of \((4)\), the corridor recursion, and \((9)\).  The uniform second-derivative bounds imply, whenever \(\widehat\vartheta\) is in the common neighborhood,
\[
 F(\widehat\vartheta)-F(\vartheta)
 =J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(\vartheta)
  (\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)+r_n,
 \qquad
 \lVert r_n\rVert
 \le C\lVert\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta\rVert^2.          \tag{10}
\]

The class \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) is contained in the compact class, so \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}compact\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\) gives uniform tightness and
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Omega(P)),
 \qquad
 \Omega(P)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}_P(g_0,g_k). \tag{11}
\]
Uniform tightness makes the neighborhood event have probability tending to one uniformly.  For each \(\epsilon>0\), on the event \(\sqrt n\lVert\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta\rVert\le K\), equation \((10)\) gives \(\sqrt n\lVert r_n\rVert\le CK^2/\sqrt n\); the complementary probability is uniformly small for large \(K\).  Hence
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}}
 P\!\left(\sqrt n\lVert r_n\rVert>\epsilon\right)
 \longrightarrow0.                                        \tag{12}
\]
Equations \((10)\)--\((12)\) prove the uniform delta-method limit
\[
 \sqrt n\{F(\widehat\vartheta)-F(\vartheta)\}
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(P)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(P)
 =J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(\vartheta)\Omega(P)
  J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(\vartheta)^\top.                      \tag{13}
\]

Let \(\widehat\Omega\) be the positive-semidefinite Isserlis estimator from \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}compact\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\).  That lemma and continuity of the localized Jacobian give
\[
 \widehat J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}-J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}
 =o_{\mathbb P}(1),
 \qquad
 \widehat\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}
 :=\widehat J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}\widehat\Omega
   \widehat J_{h,\mathrm{cor}}^\top
 =\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(P)+o_{\mathbb P}(1)              \tag{14}
\]
uniformly.  The estimate is positive semidefinite because \(\widehat\Omega\succeq0\).

We now show that the limiting target vector cannot collapse to zero, a fact needed for uniform critical-value continuity.  Define
\[
 \widetilde M_0=n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}Y_{s-1}Y_{s-1}^\top.
\]
The empirical definition gives the exact boundary identity
\[
 \widehat M_0-\widetilde M_0
 =n^{-1}(Y_nY_n^\top-Y_0Y_0^\top).                         \tag{15}
\]
The uniform fourth-moment bound implied by Gaussianity and \((3)\) makes the right side \(o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly.  From the coarse recursion in \(\mathrm{lem{:}coarse\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}reduction}\),
\[
 \widehat M_1
 =B\widetilde M_0+n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top.
\]
Using \((3)\), \((15)\), and the first-order inverse expansion gives
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}(\widehat B-B)
 =\operatorname{vec}\!\left(
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top M_0^{-1}
 \right)+o_{\mathbb P}(1)                                  \tag{16}
\]
uniformly.  The summands are martingale differences because \(\eta_s\) is independent of the preceding coarse history.  Their covariance, up to the fixed vectorization order, is
\[
 \Gamma_B=M_0^{-1}\otimes Q.                               \tag{17}
\]
The coarse covariance has the positive-semidefinite decomposition
\[
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top\succeq D\succeq d_{\min}I_d.
\]
Together with \((3)\), this yields
\[
 \Gamma_B\succeq c_BI_{d^2},
 \qquad c_B=d_{\min}/C_0>0.                                \tag{18}
\]

Because \(u\to v\in E_{uv}^{G}\), the recursion \((7)\) recovers \(A_{vu}\), and its remainder contains only strictly smaller gaps.  Those earlier coordinates cannot depend on \(B_{vu}\), while diagonal roots depend only on diagonal entries of \(B\).  Therefore
\[
 \frac{\partial A_{vu}}{\partial B_{vu}}
 =\frac{1}{C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})},
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial A_{vv}}{\partial B_{vu}}=0.                \tag{19}
\]
Since \(|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma<1\) and \(|z|=1\),
\[
 |C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|
 \le\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}|A_{vv}|^r|A_{uu}|^{m-1-r}\le m,
 \qquad
 |1-A_{vv}z|\le2.                                          \tag{20}
\]
Combining \((9)\), \((19)\), and \((20)\) gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial h_{uv}(z)}{\partial B_{vu}}\right|
 =\frac{1}{|C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|\,|1-A_{vv}z|}
 \ge\frac1{2m}.                                            \tag{21}
\]
Equations \((16)\)--\((21)\) imply that the limiting complex coordinate \(Z_h(z)\) in \((13)\) satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E_P|Z_h(z)|^2\ge\frac{c_B}{4m^2}>0               \tag{22}
\]
uniformly for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\).  Thus the limiting real covariance may change rank across the class, but it is never the zero matrix.  This conclusion does not require \(A_{vu}\ne0\).

For a real vector arranged in complex-coordinate pairs define
\[
 \lVert x\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}
 =\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt{x_{\Re,z}^2+x_{\Im,z}^2}.
\]
For \(\Sigma\succeq0\), let \(Z_\Sigma\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) and define
\[
 c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma)
 =\inf\{t:\Pr(\lVert Z_\Sigma\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\le t)
 \ge1-\alpha\}.                                           \tag{23}
\]
The assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}confidence\mbox{-}level}\) gives \(0<1-\alpha<1\).  The covariance range in \((13)\) is compact by continuity of the ingredients and compactness of the parameter class; equation \((22)\) keeps it away from the zero matrix.  On the support subspace of any nonzero centered Gaussian vector, the Gaussian law has a positive density and the restriction of \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\) is a norm.  Every norm sphere has Lebesgue measure zero in that subspace, while every nonempty norm annulus has positive measure.  Hence the distribution function in \((23)\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), with no atom at zero, and its \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile is unique and positive.

If \(\Sigma_j\to\Sigma\), use a common \(\xi\sim N(0,I)\) and the continuous positive-semidefinite square root to couple
\[
 Z_{\Sigma_j}=\Sigma_j^{1/2}\xi
 \longrightarrow \Sigma^{1/2}\xi=Z_\Sigma
 \quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
At two continuity points bracketing the unique quantile, convergence in distribution sandwiches the quantiles, proving
\[
 c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_j)\longrightarrow c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma). \tag{24}
\]
Compactness makes this continuity uniform on a neighborhood of the covariance range.  With
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}
 =c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}),
\]
equations \((14)\) and \((24)\) give
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}
 =c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(P))+o_{\mathbb P}(1) \tag{25}
\]
uniformly.

Suppose uniform coverage failed.  There would then exist a sequence \(P_n\in\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) along which the absolute coverage error stayed bounded away from zero.  Compactness supplies a subsequence whose fine parameters converge, and continuity gives \(\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}}(P_n)\to\Sigma_*\ne0\).  Along this subsequence, \((13)\) gives convergence of the centered statistic to \(N(0,\Sigma_*)\), while \((25)\) gives convergence in probability of the critical value to \(c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_*)\).  The boundary
\[
 \{x:\lVert x\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}
 =c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_*)\}
\]
has zero limiting probability by the sphere argument above.  Therefore
\[
 P_{P_n}\!\left\{
 \max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt n\,
 |\widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}(z)-h_{uv}(z)|
 \le\widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}
 \right\}\longrightarrow1-\alpha,                         \tag{26}
\]
contradicting the selected sequence.  The event in \((26)\) is exactly the simultaneous-disk event in the statement.  This proves uniform coverage using only target-corridor separation and without selecting any off-corridor branch.

proposed.name: directed target corridor
proposed.construction:
Allow a directed path of length zero at either endpoint and define
\[
 V_{uv}^{G}
 =\{w\in V:u\leadsto w\text{ in }G\text{ and }w\leadsto v\text{ in }G\},
 \qquad
 E_{uv}^{G}
 =\{j\to i\in E:j\in V_{uv}^{G},\ i\in V_{uv}^{G}\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(V_{uv}^{G}\) and \(E_{uv}^{G}\) are respectively the vertices and edges lying on at least one directed path from \(u\) to \(v\).

proposed.name: target-corridor root and transfer map
proposed.construction:
For odd \(m\), define the partial corridor-root map \(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)\) as follows.  For each \(i\in V_{uv}^{G}\), set
\[
 \mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m},
\]
where the real odd root is used.  Process the edges \(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}\) in increasing order of \(i-j\), treating graph-forbidden entries as zero, and set
\[
 \mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{ij}
 =\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B))}
 {C_m(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{ii},\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{jj})}.
\]
The map is defined precisely when all displayed denominators are nonzero.  Its transfer functional is
\[
 \Phi_{uv,m,G}(B)(z)
 =\frac{\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{vu}z}
 {1-\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}(B)_{vv}z}.
\]

proposed.name: target-corridor derivative-separated class
proposed.construction:
The target-corridor derivative-separated class is
\[
\begin{split}
 \mathcal M_{uv,\mathrm{cor}}^{\partial}
 &(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)\\
 ={}&\left\{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max}):
 m\text{ is odd},\right.\\
 &\left.\qquad
 \min_{i\in V_{uv}^{G}}m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa,
 \quad
 \min_{j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}}|C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa
 \right\}.
\end{split}
\]
The minima are over nonempty finite sets whenever \(u\to v\in G\), because then \(u,v\in V_{uv}^{G}\) and \(u\to v\in E_{uv}^{G}\).

proposed.name: target-corridor recursive plug-in estimator
proposed.construction:

\[
 \widehat B=\widehat M_1\widehat M_0^{-1},
 \qquad
 \widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}(z)
 =\Phi_{uv,m,G}(\widehat B)(z),\qquad z\in\mathcal Z,
\]
using only the diagonal and edge operations in \(\mathscr R_{uv,m,G}\).  Define the estimator arbitrarily if \(\widehat M_0\) is not positive definite or a corridor denominator vanishes.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Inference on the larger localized class must use only the uniquely recoverable corridor rather than a global branch.

proposed.statement:
Suppose \(\mathcal Z\ne\varnothing\), \(m\) is odd, every arrow \(j\to i\) in \(G\) satisfies \(j<i\), \(u\to v\in G\), and
\[
 \kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}.
\]
Then the derivative-separated regular class \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)\) is nonempty.  Uniformly over this class, as \(n\to\infty\), the real vector stacking the real and imaginary parts of
\[
 \sqrt n\bigl(\widehat h_{uv}(z)-h_{uv}(z)\bigr),
 \qquad z\in\mathcal Z,
\]
converges to the centered Gaussian law obtained by applying the Jacobian of the moment-to-root recursion and
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z\,\mathrm dA_{vu}}{1-A_{vv}z}
  +\frac{A_{vu}z^2\,\mathrm dA_{vv}}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}
\]
to the long-run Gaussian lag-moment covariance.  Let \(\widehat\Sigma_h\) be the positive-semidefinite plug-in estimate obtained from the Gaussian Isserlis covariance series and the recursive Jacobian, and let \(\widehat c_{1-\alpha}\) be the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the maximum complex modulus of the corresponding centered Gaussian vector.  Then
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}}
 \left|
 P\!\left\{
 h_{uv}(z)\in
 \left\{w\in\mathbb C:
 |w-\widehat h_{uv}(z)|\le
 \frac{\widehat c_{1-\alpha}}{\sqrt n}
 \right\}
 \text{ for every }z\in\mathcal Z
 \right\}-(1-\alpha)
 \right|\longrightarrow0,
\]
where the class in the supremum has the full argument list displayed above.
proposed.justification: The original globally separated class remains useful as a simple sufficient regime and is now an explicit corollary of the sharper target-corridor theorem.
proposed.gap: Existing fine-grid process-graph Wald theory does not treat the aliased root Jacobian; the corridor theorem further shows that nuisance branches outside directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) paths need no separation.
proposed.consumer: Researchers may use the familiar global separation check, while the sharper theorem permits Wald disks whenever only the target corridor is regular.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Retain the global regular Wald statement while making its proof spine an explicit corollary of target-corridor inference.

proposed.comparator_claim: Gong et al. obtain positive fine-model recovery under non-Gaussian innovations together with full-rank, nonzero-diagonal, and weak-connectivity conditions, and separately note generic nonuniqueness under Gaussian data.
We present a unifying framework for parameter identifiability and estimation under both subsampling and mixed frequencies when the shocks are non-Gaussian.
The algorithm forms a Schur decomposition and computes a \(p\)-th root of the triangular factor by a recursion.
The spectral latent-factor half-trek criterion identifies direct link functions by rational operations on the spectral density.
We characterise the asymptotic distribution of causal effect and spectral contribution estimators in terms of algebraic relations dictated by the process graph.
We establish useful deviation bounds for dependent Gaussian data using a spectral measure of stability.
We prove an exponential probability tail inequality for positive semidefinite quadratic forms in a subgaussian random vector.
The results about coverage probability are stated in a nonasymptotic way and apply for small and moderate sample size.
We provide a constraint satisfaction procedure for system-timescale causal structures corresponding to a measurement-timescale structure.
Classical CAD projection algorithms preserve chordal structure when projection follows a perfect elimination ordering.
In the regular mixed-frequency VARMA case with moving-average order exceeding autoregressive order, generic local identification fails.

prose_updates.tldr: Subsampling turns a fine-grid process DAG into a matrix-root problem, so a queried causal transfer is governed by the complete compatible fiber rather than by a selected numerical root. For odd \(m\), the transfer is identified and smoothly recoverable when diagonal-root derivatives and divided differences are separated only on vertices and edges lying on directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) paths; the earlier globally separated Wald theorem is a corollary. For even \(m\), the same-law sign obstruction holds on the larger class of all stable Gaussian VAR(1) transitions with arbitrary positive-definite innovation covariance, without an order or triangularity assumption. Exact transfer-aware certification and branch-free confidence-region inversion cover singular and nonregular cases.

project_justification.gap: Published subsampling results either use non-Gaussian shocks for positive recovery, enumerate qualitative graph equivalence classes, or choose a numerical matrix-root branch. Gong et al.'s positive theorem assumes non-Gaussian innovations together with full-rank, nonzero-diagonal, and weak-connectivity conditions, so neither it nor the present Gaussian supplied-order result contains the other. No prior result identifies and infers a queried Gaussian transfer using only its directed target corridor while retaining exact ambiguity certificates elsewhere.
project_justification.niche: A supplied causal order makes triangular divided-difference recursion available, but a direct transfer needs only the vertices and edges on directed paths from \(u\) to \(v\). Localizing root-derivative and divided-difference separation to that corridor avoids regularity assumptions on irrelevant branches. Diagonal fine innovations remain informative for complete-fiber certification, whereas the even-factor global sign calculation needs neither triangularity nor diagonal innovations.
project_justification.fill: The project gives an explicit target-corridor identifying map and simultaneous Wald disks on a nonempty compact corridor-separated odd class, with the globally separated theorem retained as a corollary. It also gives an unrestricted stable-Gaussian even-sign obstruction with arbitrary positive-definite innovations, plus a total transfer-aware CAD fallback with attained witnesses and finite-sample branch-free inversion. The covariance-envelope fallback remains a validity device equal pathwise to the deterministic box, not a claimed adaptive improvement.

sampling_model.design: The main identifying and certification class is a single stationary Gaussian fine-grid VAR(1), observed at times \(0,m,\ldots,nm\), with known \(m\), supplied labeled process DAG \(G\), triangular transition, and diagonal fine innovation covariance. The even-factor sign corollary is deliberately broader: it permits an arbitrary stable transition and arbitrary positive-definite Gaussian innovation covariance and needs no supplied order.
sampling_model.units: The sampling units are the \(n+1\) dependent coarse-time vectors \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)\).
sampling_model.treatment: There is no binary treatment; the causal query is the direct fine-grid transfer along the supplied process edge \(u\to v\).
sampling_model.overlap: There is no treatment-overlap condition. The stability margin gives \(|1-A_{vv}z|\ge\gamma>0\) on \(\mathbb T\), which is the support condition needed for the rational transfer.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Estimate \((M_0,M_1)\) by overlapping empirical lag moments and form \(\widehat B=\widehat M_1\widehat M_0^{-1}\). On the odd target-corridor class, recover only the diagonal and edge coordinates on directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) paths, propagate the Isserlis long-run covariance through that localized Jacobian, and report simultaneous Wald disks. The global derivative-separated estimator agrees on the target and is a corollary. Outside the localized regular class, invert the rationally outward-rounded moment box through all compatible fine-grid branches without selecting one.

prose_updates.related_work: Gong et al. (2015) motivate temporal causal recovery from subsampled data. Their positive recovery theorem uses non-Gaussian innovations together with full-rank, nonzero-diagonal, and weak-connectivity conditions; the present positive result instead uses Gaussian innovations, a supplied order, and process-DAG restrictions, so the two positive classes are incomparable rather than related by inclusion. Their Gaussian nonuniqueness discussion motivates the obstruction, while the present proof isolates an even-factor sign pair on the strictly larger stable Gaussian VAR(1) class with arbitrary positive-definite innovation covariance and no order or triangularity requirement. Tank, Fox, and Shojaie (2019) likewise use non-Gaussian shocks and likelihood methods. Hyttinen et al. (2017) preserve qualitative subsampling ambiguity through exact constraints, whereas the present target is a numerical rational transfer. Smith (2003), Bini, Higham, and Meini (2005), and Higham (2008) supply triangular-root algorithms and branch theory; the new step localizes recursion to directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) paths and then combines graph zeros, innovation covariance, transfer equality, and complete-fiber certification. Reiter et al. (2026) identify rational link effects from an unaliased fine-grid spectrum, and Reiter et al. (2024) derive local delta-method inference once fine-grid coefficients are differentiably estimable. Basu and Michailidis (2015), Hsu, Kakade, and Zhang (2012), and Giurcanu and Spokoiny (2004) provide concentration context for finite-sample moment regions. Mixed-frequency VARMA and unit-root results of Deistler, Koelbl, and Anderson (2017), Anderson et al. (2016), and Gersing, Sögner, and Deistler (2023) concern different model classes.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The target-corridor result still assumes a supplied scientifically defensible order and an odd known sampling factor for positive identification; it does not infer the order. Genericity is in fine-parameter space, not observed-law image space. Exact CAD certifies termination but not polynomial-time scalability, and executable witnesses require effective real-closed-field input. Gong et al.'s Temperature--Ozone example is used only as a conditional \(m=2\) Gaussian ambiguity audit if external science supplies the one-way order; their fit does not establish that order, and their positive non-Gaussian theorem is not imported into this Gaussian class.
prose_updates.honest_scope: Positive identification and Wald inference concern stable, ordered, finite-dimensional Gaussian VAR(1) process-DAG models with known odd subsampling factor and diagonal fine innovation covariance. Point identification of \(h_{uv}\) and smooth recovery require noncollision and derivative separation only on the directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) corridor; coefficients and innovation variances outside that corridor may remain ambiguous, and no full-matrix uniqueness is claimed from localized conditions. The older global derivative-separated class is a nonempty sufficient subclass when \(\kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\). In contrast, the even-factor sign obstruction holds for every stable Gaussian VAR(1) with arbitrary positive-definite innovation covariance, even without a supplied order, triangularity, or graph zeros, whenever the queried coordinate is nonzero. Outside the corridor-regular class, inference is branch-free. No claim is made about unknown sampling factors, high-dimensional rates, VARMA or unit-root extensions, or the scientific validity of the Temperature--Ozone ordering.

proofs.proof_tex:
Assume that \(m\) is even and fix \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}known\mbox{-}sampling\mbox{-}factor}\), \(m\ge2\) is the fixed sampling factor, so \(m=2k\) for an integer \(k\ge1\).  Put \(\widetilde A=-A\).  The first equality in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) gives \(A^m=B\), and therefore
\[
 \widetilde A^m=(-A)^{2k}=A^{2k}=B.
\]
For every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\),
\[
 \widetilde A^rD(\widetilde A^r)^\top
 =(-1)^rA^rD\bigl((-1)^rA^r\bigr)^\top
 =(-1)^{2r}A^rD(A^r)^\top
 =A^rD(A^r)^\top.
\]
Summing this equality and using the second equality in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\) yields
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\widetilde A^rD(\widetilde A^r)^\top
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
 =Q.
\]
Every required zero is preserved because \(\widetilde A_{ij}=-A_{ij}\): thus \(\widetilde A_{ij}=0\) when \(i<j\), and also when \(i>j\) and \(j\to i\notin G\).  Stability is preserved coordinatewise since
\[
 \max_i|\widetilde A_{ii}|=\max_i|A_{ii}|<1.
\]
The matrix \(D\) is unchanged, so it remains diagonal and positive definite.  These are all constraints in \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\), and hence
\[
 (-A,D)=(\widetilde A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G).
\]

The same membership conditions also show that \(A\) is lower triangular.  Its characteristic polynomial is therefore
\[
 \det(\lambda I-A)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\lambda-A_{ii}),
\]
so \(\rho(A)=\max_i|A_{ii}|<1\).  The theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}unrestricted\mbox{-}even\mbox{-}sign\mbox{-}ambiguity}\), applied with this \(A\), the positive-definite matrix \(D\), and the even factor \(m\), now proves that the stationary Gaussian processes with fine transitions \(A\) and \(-A\) have exactly the same sampled law.  This application is valid a fortiori for diagonal \(D\); the unrestricted theorem itself does not use that restriction.

By \(\mathrm{ass{:}query\mbox{-}edge}\), \(u\to v\) is the queried arrow.  Write \(p=A_{vu}\) and \(q=A_{vv}\).  From the two established memberships and \(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}fiber}\), the common observed law attains both
\[
 h_+(z)=\frac{pz}{1-qz}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 h_-(z)=\frac{-pz}{1+qz}
\]
in \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\).  Here \(|q|<1\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}compatible\mbox{-}fiber}\), so both denominators are nonzero for every \(|z|=1\).  If the two rational functions were equal, cross multiplication would imply
\[
 pz(1+qz)=-pz(1-qz),
\]
and cancellation of the quadratic terms would give \(2pz=0\).  This is impossible when \(p=A_{vu}\ne0\).  Hence the transfer fiber contains two attained unequal elements.  Since they arise from the same Gaussian coarse law, no functional of that law can equal the queried nonzero transfer in both compatible models; point identification fails.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(m\) be even, let \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) satisfy \(\rho(A)<1\), and let \(D\in\mathbb S_{++}^{d}\) be arbitrary.  For each \(s\in\{-1,1\}\), let \((X_t^{(s)})_{t\in\mathbb Z}\) be the zero-mean stationary Gaussian VAR(1) model
\[
 X_t^{(s)}=sA X_{t-1}^{(s)}+\varepsilon_t^{(s)},
 \qquad
 (\varepsilon_t^{(s)})_{t\in\mathbb Z}\mathrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim N(0,D).
\]
Then the subsampled processes \((X_{jm}^{(1)})_{j\in\mathbb Z}\) and \((X_{jm}^{(-1)})_{j\in\mathbb Z}\) have the same law.  This conclusion requires neither a supplied variable order, triangularity or graph-support restrictions on \(A\), nor diagonality of \(D\).  For any \(u\ne v\) such that \(A_{vu}\ne0\), the attained direct coordinate transfers
\[
 \frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{-A_{vu}z}{1+A_{vv}z}
\]
are unequal as elements of \(\mathbb R(z)\).  Consequently the direct coordinate transfer is not point identified by the even-subsampled stationary Gaussian law on this unrestricted stable VAR(1) class.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(A_s=sA\) for \(s\in\{-1,1\}\).  First we verify that the stationary models in the statement are well defined.  Choose \(\varrho\) with \(\rho(A)<\varrho<1\).  A finite-dimensional Jordan-form calculation gives a constant \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
 \lVert A^k\rVert\le C \varrho^k,
 \qquad k\ge0.
\]
Indeed, on a Jordan block with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), every entry of its \(k\)-th power is a constant multiple of \(\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}\) for some fixed \(j\); since \(|\lambda|<\varrho\), each such sequence is bounded by a constant times \(\varrho^k\).  Conjugating the finitely many blocks changes only the constant.  The same bound holds for \(A_s^k=s^kA^k\).  Taking \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) to be the spectral norm, independence and centering of the innovations therefore imply, for \(M>N\),
\[
 \mathbb E\left\lVert
   \sum_{k=N}^{M}A_s^k\varepsilon_{t-k}^{(s)}
 \right\rVert^2
 =\sum_{k=N}^{M}\operatorname{tr}
   \left(A_s^kD(A_s^k)^\top\right)
 \le \operatorname{tr}(D)C^2\sum_{k=N}^{M}\varrho^{2k}.
\]
The last expression tends to zero as \(N\to\infty\), uniformly in \(M>N\).  Thus
\[
 X_t^{(s)}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}A_s^k\varepsilon_{t-k}^{(s)}
\]
converges in second mean, is centered, stationary, and Gaussian, and shifting the series proves
\(X_t^{(s)}=A_sX_{t-1}^{(s)}+\varepsilon_t^{(s)}\).

Iterating this recursion through one block of length \(m\), and defining \(Y_j^{(s)}:=X_{jm}^{(s)}\), gives
\[
 Y_j^{(s)}=A_s^mY_{j-1}^{(s)}+\eta_j^{(s)},
 \qquad
 \eta_j^{(s)}:=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_s^r\varepsilon_{jm-r}^{(s)}.
\]
Distinct indices \(j\) use disjoint innovation blocks.  Hence the \(\eta_j^{(s)}\) are independent centered Gaussian vectors, and \(\eta_j^{(s)}\) is independent of the sigma-field generated by \(Y_{j-1}^{(s)},Y_{j-2}^{(s)},\ldots\).  Because \(m\) is even,
\[
 A_s^m=s^mA^m=A^m=:\overline B.
\]
Moreover, symmetry of scalar multiplication with matrix transposition yields, term by term,
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(\eta_j^{(s)})
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(sA)^rD\bigl((sA)^r\bigr)^\top
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}s^{2r}A^rD(A^r)^\top
 =\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
 =:\overline Q.
\]
Notice that \(\overline Q\succ0\), because its \(r=0\) summand is \(D\succ0\) and every other summand is positive semidefinite.  Also \(\rho(\overline B)=\rho(A)^m<1\).  Iteration of the coarse recursion through \(L\) blocks gives
\[
 Y_0^{(s)}=\overline B^L Y_{-L}^{(s)}
 +\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\overline B^\ell\eta_{-\ell}^{(s)}.
\]
Stationarity gives \(\mathbb E\lVert Y_{-L}^{(s)}\rVert^2=\mathbb E\lVert Y_0^{(s)}\rVert^2<\infty\), while the same matrix-power bound applied to \(\overline B\) implies \(\overline B^L Y_{-L}^{(s)}\to0\) in second mean.  Taking \(L\to\infty\) shows that its stationary marginal covariance is uniquely
\[
 \overline\Gamma_0
 =\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\overline B^\ell
      \overline Q(\overline B^\ell)^\top.
\]
Thus both sampled processes have initial distribution \(N(0,\overline\Gamma_0)\), conditional transition kernel
\[
 Y_j\mid Y_{j-1}=y\sim N(\overline B y,\overline Q),
\]
and independent block innovations.  Iterated conditioning proves equality of every finite-dimensional distribution, hence equality of the two sampled-process laws.  None of this calculation imposed an ordering, a zero restriction on \(A\), or diagonality of \(D\).

Finally, set \(p=A_{vu}\) and \(q=A_{vv}\).  The direct coordinate transfers under \(A\) and \(-A\) are respectively
\[
 h_+(z)=\frac{pz}{1-qz},
 \qquad
 h_-(z)=\frac{-pz}{1+qz}.
\]
Their denominator polynomials have constant term one and hence are nonzero polynomials.  If \(h_+=h_-\) in \(\mathbb R(z)\), cross multiplication would give
\[
 pz(1+qz)=-pz(1-qz),
\]
so cancellation of the equal quadratic terms would give \(2pz=0\) as a polynomial.  This contradicts \(p=A_{vu}\ne0\).  The same observed law therefore attains two unequal values of the causal query, which is precisely failure of point identification.

proposed.statement: If \(m\) is even and \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), then \((-A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\). If \(A_{vu}\ne0\), the two attained transfers \(A_{vu}z/(1-A_{vv}z)\) and \(-A_{vu}z/(1+A_{vv}z)\) are unequal as rational functions. Hence no nonzero queried edge transfer is point identified from the Gaussian coarse law under an even factor.
proposed.justification: The global sign action is an unavoidable same-law obstruction that covariance filtering cannot remove.
proposed.gap: Gong et al.'s even sign conclusion is embedded in a non-Gaussian identification theorem; this claim proves the obstruction directly for the Gaussian law after the complete coarse covariance restriction.
proposed.consumer: For a conditionally ordered Temperature--Ozone analysis with \(m=2\), the result prevents reporting a branch-selected directional transfer as identified.
